concepts.title: What Is a Drug?
concepts.contentHtml:
A drug is a molecule that produces a desired biological effect — usually by binding to a specific protein and modulating its activity.

Most drugs are small molecules (~500 Da). Some are biologics: antibodies, proteins, RNA. The molecular target is usually an enzyme, receptor, ion channel, or transporter.

Roughly 15,000 drugs are approved worldwide. They target a few hundred distinct protein families. The druggable genome — proteins amenable to small-molecule modulation — is estimated at ~3000 of the ~20,000 human proteins.

concepts.title: Receptors and Affinity
concepts.contentHtml:
Drugs bind to their targets via specific interactions — hydrogen bonds, van der Waals, hydrophobic packing, charge interactions. The binding is reversible (mostly).

Affinity is measured by the dissociation constant K_d — the concentration at which half the receptor sites are occupied. Tight binders have K_d in the nanomolar range; weak ones micromolar or worse.

Selectivity matters: a good drug binds its target much more tightly than off-targets. Off-target binding causes side effects.

concepts.title: Agonists, Antagonists, and Inhibitors
concepts.contentHtml:
Different drugs work in different ways:

• Agonist: binds receptor and activates it (e.g., morphine on opioid receptors).
• Antagonist: binds receptor but does not activate; blocks the natural agonist (naloxone reverses opioid overdoses).
• Inhibitor: blocks an enzyme's active site (statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase).
• Modulator: alters activity allosterically without competing at the active site.

title: Drug Discovery Pipeline
description: From an idea to a pill

concepts.title: Target Identification & Validation
concepts.contentHtml:
The first step: identify a protein whose modulation should treat a disease. Validation requires showing that altering the target's activity has the desired effect — through genetics, animal models, or human disease association.

Genome-wide association studies, knockout mice, and CRISPR screens have transformed target identification in the last decade.

concepts.title: Hit-to-Lead-to-Candidate
concepts.contentHtml:
Hit: an initial active molecule from a screen (often micromolar IC₅₀, weak but real). High-throughput screening of compound libraries (often >10⁶ molecules) finds hits.

Lead: an optimized hit with reasonable potency, selectivity, and properties. Medicinal chemists modify the structure iteratively.

Candidate: the molecule chosen to enter human trials. By this point it has been optimized for potency, selectivity, ADMET, and synthesizability.

concepts.title: Clinical Trials
concepts.contentHtml:
Drugs progress through three (sometimes four) phases of clinical trials:

Phase I: ~20-100 healthy volunteers; safety and pharmacokinetics.
Phase II: ~100-300 patients; efficacy and dose-finding.
Phase III: ~1,000-10,000 patients; large-scale efficacy and safety.
Phase IV: post-approval surveillance.

Roughly 10% of drugs that enter Phase I make it to approval. The full process takes 10-15 years and costs ~$2.6 billion (industry average, with high variance).

title: ADMET
description: What the body does to a drug

concepts.title: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion
concepts.contentHtml:
ADME describes a drug's journey through the body:

• Absorption: from gut to bloodstream (for oral drugs). Affected by solubility and permeability.
• Distribution: through tissues. Lipophilic drugs partition into fat; some don't cross the blood-brain barrier.
• Metabolism: liver enzymes (especially CYP450 family) modify drugs to facilitate excretion.
• Excretion: kidneys (urine) and liver (bile/feces) clear drugs.

Add T for toxicity → ADMET. A drug must clear all of these hurdles.

concepts.title: Lipinski's Rule of Five
concepts.contentHtml:
Christopher Lipinski analyzed thousands of drugs and oral failures (1997) and noted patterns. The Rule of Five: for good oral bioavailability, prefer molecules with

• Molecular weight ≤ 500
• logP ≤ 5 (not too lipophilic)
• ≤ 5 hydrogen bond donors
• ≤ 10 hydrogen bond acceptors

Heuristic, not law. Drugs that violate the rules can still work (paclitaxel does), but the failure rate is higher. Modern medicinal chemists internalize this — most candidate molecules respect it.

concepts.title: Drug-Drug Interactions
concepts.contentHtml:
Cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolize most drugs. CYP3A4 alone handles ~50% of marketed drugs.

If two drugs share a CYP, one can inhibit metabolism of the other — unsafe drug levels result. Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 in the gut, dramatically affecting bioavailability of many drugs.

Pharmacogenomics: genetic variation in CYPs and transporters explains why some patients respond well and others toxically to the same dose. Personalized dosing is increasingly common in oncology and psychiatry.

concepts.title: Structure-Based Drug Design
concepts.contentHtml:
Solve the X-ray (or now cryo-EM) structure of the target protein. Identify the active site. Design molecules that fit precisely.

Major successes: HIV protease inhibitors (saquinavir and successors transformed AIDS into a manageable disease); the BCR-ABL inhibitor imatinib (Gleevec) for chronic myeloid leukemia.

AlphaFold has effectively given the field the protein structure of every target — accelerating SBDD enormously.

concepts.title: Fragment-Based Lead Discovery
concepts.contentHtml:
Instead of screening complete drug-like molecules, screen tiny fragments (~150 Da). Fragments bind weakly (mM affinity) but characterize binding pockets sub-site by sub-site.

Then merge or grow fragments into a fully-formed lead. Far smaller libraries (~1000 fragments) provide the same diverse binding-mode information as million-compound HTS libraries — but with better starting points.

Has produced approved drugs (e.g. vemurafenib for melanoma, venetoclax for leukemia) and shifted lead-discovery practice substantially since the 2000s.

concepts.title: Computational Drug Design
concepts.contentHtml:
Docking, molecular dynamics, and free-energy perturbation predict binding modes and affinities. ML-based pose and affinity predictors are integrated alongside.

Generative models propose new molecules with target properties; physics-based filters validate. The pipeline is increasingly closed-loop — propose, predict, synthesize, test, learn.

AI-discovered candidates first entered clinical trials around 2020; Insilico Medicine's INS018_055 (for lung fibrosis) reached Phase II in 2023. The field is just getting going.

concepts.title: Biologics
concepts.contentHtml:
Biologics are large molecules — antibodies, recombinant proteins, peptides. Antibodies (humira, rituximab, dozens more) target specific extracellular proteins with exquisite selectivity.

Biologics dominate revenue at most major pharma companies. They're also more expensive and complex to manufacture than small molecules — and require injection rather than oral dosing.

Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) deliver cytotoxic payloads selectively to tumor cells via a tumor-targeting antibody. A new generation of cancer drugs.

concepts.title: RNA & Gene Therapy
concepts.contentHtml:
mRNA as a drug: deliver mRNA encoding a protein (vaccine antigen, replacement enzyme) — let the body produce it. COVID vaccines (Pfizer/BioNTech, Moderna) proved the platform at scale in 2020-2021.

siRNA drugs (patisiran for amyloidosis, others) silence specific gene expression. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) block mRNA translation or alter splicing.

Gene therapy delivers a working copy of a gene via viral vector. Approved for spinal muscular atrophy, hemophilia, and sickle cell disease (CRISPR-edited Casgevy, 2023). Cures, not just treatments — at single-dose seven-figure prices, for now.

concepts.title: Targeted Protein Degradation
concepts.contentHtml:
Traditional drugs inhibit proteins. PROTACs (proteolysis-targeting chimeras) instead destroy them — bifunctional molecules that recruit a cell's own ubiquitin ligase to tag a target for proteasomal degradation.

Advantages: a single PROTAC can degrade many copies of a target (catalytic, not stoichiometric); can address 'undruggable' targets that lack good binding pockets.

Multiple PROTACs are in clinical trials. Molecular glues — small molecules that induce protein-protein interactions for degradation — are an adjacent and rapidly growing class.
